title: Ignorance or Incompetence? Building Agent Tasks That Tell the Difference
hook: When an agent fails a professional task, was it incapable or just missing a convention nobody published? This protocol splits the instruction from the private knowledge so you can test which.
key_points: Real professional work depends on conventions absent from public corpora; benchmarks rarely control whether the agent has them.
The protocol separates a task instruction from a compact artefact holding private conventions, reference tables, and utility operators.
Task instructions are byte-identical in the provided- and withheld-artefact conditions, so only knowledge differs.
Provenance records, leak audits, and executable witnesses make the dependence on the artefact explicit and testable.
Across fifteen calibration tasks one frontier agent config passed 68.0% with the artefact and 0% without; a plausible-but-wrong artefact also yielded 0%.
The authors are explicit that this validates the construction protocol, not that the tasks improve post-training.
content_html: An agent flubs a professional task. Two very different explanations look identical from the outside: it lacked a convention that only exists inside some firm's internal docs, or it simply couldn't do the work. Tian and colleagues point out that benchmarks almost never control for this — and propose a construction protocol that does.
extra_html:
How it works

Each task splits in two: an instruction, and a compact artefact containing the private conventions, reference tables, and utility operators the task depends on. The agent is then run in two conditions, with the artefact provided and withheld, using byte-identical instructions so nothing but the knowledge changes. Construction-time provenance, leak audits, and executable witnesses make the dependence explicit and checkable. Deterministic solvers and rule corpora give exact ground truth for structured tasks; named criterion-level rubrics cover outputs no single executable oracle can check.

Why it matters

Across fifteen calibration tasks, the authors report one frontier agent configuration passing 68.0% with the artefact and 0% without — and on one task, a plausible but incorrect artefact also yielded 0% across five trials, evidence the agent was really using the content. A configuration-relative screen retained seven tasks meeting their five-trial knowledge-gating criterion. The authors are careful about scope: these experiments validate the protocol's behavior, not a claim that the retained tasks improve post-training. Part of the suite and tooling is released publicly.

related.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability?
related.hook: An agent score only means something if the task still requires the skill it claims to test. Auditing 2,385 traces, two-thirds showed the agent taking a shortcut instead.

flashcards.prompt: Why must the task instruction be byte-identical across the provided- and withheld-artefact conditions?
flashcards.back_html: So the only difference between conditions is access to the private knowledge. Any wording change would confound ignorance with a different task.

flashcards.prompt: What does a 68.0% pass rate with the artefact and 0% without it demonstrate about a task?

choices.text: The task genuinely depends on the private knowledge — it is knowledge-gated, not just hard
The agent is incompetent at the task regardless of knowledge
The artefact leaked the answers into the instruction
The task is too easy to be useful

flashcards.explanation_html: Solvable with the artefact and unsolvable without it is exactly the signature of a knowledge gate. Leak audits and executable witnesses are what rule out the artefact simply containing answers.

flashcards.prompt: What did giving the agent a plausible but incorrect artefact reveal?
flashcards.back_html: On one task it also produced 0% across five trials — the agent was genuinely relying on the artefact's content, not just on its presence as a cue.
